items.body: The rotunda of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) When two mental health clinic owners in Idaho set out to restore critical services for people with severe mental illness, they faced an uphill battle. The Idaho Legislature was gearing up for across-the-board budget cuts. But Laura Scuri and Ric Boyce armed lawmakers with information and data — and spent time talking to journalists when four patients died after the mobile treatment service had been cut. Ric Boyce, director of Mental Health Specialists, testifies before the Idaho Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel on Dec. 15, 2025 in Rexburg. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The two often worked behind the scenes, directly with lawmakers instead of testifying before committees. “We formed individual relationships with half the Legislature pretty much,” Boyce recalled in an interview. In the end, the programs that they advocated served as a rare instance of a budget cut that state lawmakers reversed. On the final day of this year’s legislative session, Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed into law a bill that temporarily restored funding for the programs that the two providers pushed for: the Assertive Community Treatment program, a mobile program for people with severe mental illness, and peer support services, which helps people navigate treatment. After four patients died, Idaho governor approves restoring cut Medicaid mental health programs Now, a mental health nonprofit plans to honor the two. Next month, the National Alliance on Mental Illness of Idaho plans to award them both the Kathie Garrett Impact Award, named after a former Idaho lawmaker. In a news release, the nonprofit said the duo’s advocacy “led to the return of those programs.” The award came as a surprise. “I don’t think either one of us were thinking for a second it’s something that would be noticed,” said Boyce, a clinical social worker who owns Mental Health Specialists, a clinic in eastern Idaho’s Chubbuck. “What was important to us was that we were able to get the clients we were working with back into the program they needed so badly. And that was enough.” Scuri, who co-owns Access Behavioral Health Services in Boise, said it’s her first award. “So it’s extra special to me — especially with the environment that we’re in, and all the changes,” she said. But he said this experience tested that conception. “What I learned was that there are ways to make change happen even when it seems hopeless,” he said. But to do that, he said, requires a lot of work — and help. While he and Scuri were talking with lawmakers, he said they also found lawmakers coming to them for answers — to questions raised by community members in letters and direct outreach on all sorts of Medicaid changes, not just the cuts they were focused on. “Even individual advocacy, of sending a single letter, cumulatively had an effect. And those things were changing the minds of legislators,” Boyce said. Laura Scuri, co-owner of Access Behavioral Health Services, testifies before the Idaho Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel in Rexburg on Dec. 15, 2025. items.body: A nine-member committee will begin the search for a new University of Idaho president . The State Board of Education announced the committee Friday, marking the first significant public step in the search. Current U of I President C. Scott Green announced his retirement on Sept. 9 ; he will stay on as president at his alma mater until June 30. Two State Board members will head the search: Shawn Keough of Sandpoint will chair the committee, and Pete Koehler of Caldwell will serve as vice chair. Koehler is a U of I alum. Here’s a look at the rest of the committee members: Chandra Zenner Ford, the U of I’s senior associate to the president, and executive officer of the university’s Boise and Southwest Idaho center. Mya Pronschinske Groza, a U of I marketing professor, and associate dean of the College of Business and Economics. Bill Gilbert, a former State Board member and a 1997 U of I graduate. Phil Reberger, who served as chief of staff to former Idaho Gov. and Sen. Dirk Kempthorne and former Idaho Sen. Steve Symms. Reberger is a 1964 U of I graduate. Clint Marshall, chair of the University of Idaho Foundation. Mary Hasenoehrl, owner of GKH Farms and partner in Gross Farms, Wilder. Dave Whitehead, president of Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories, Pullman, Wash. “We are grateful to these Vandals and community leaders for agreeing to serve,” State Board President Kurt Liebich said in a news release. “President Green has put the university in a strong position, and we are committed to a thorough search that finds a leader who can build on that momentum.” The timetable for the search is not set. However, the U of I has said the State Board hopes to fill the post by spring, before Green’s retirement. Under a new state law , passed this year, the presidential search process is now almost entirely a closed-door process. After private meetings and interviews, the search committee will submit a sole finalist’s name to the State Board. If board members agree to the recommendation, the board can publicly name the finalist and make the hire within 10 business days. The law also sets the guidelines for the makeup of a search committee, composed of at least eight members. With nine members, the U of I committee is slightly larger than the minimum required by law.

(Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) As the Nov. 3 general election nears, rumors have cropped up that a never-used, 1917 Idaho state law could be used to circumvent the race for U.S. Senate. U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, delivers remarks during the Virginia-class nuclear-powered fast-attack submarine USS Idaho’s commissioning ceremony at Naval Submarine Base New London in Groton, Connecticut, on April 25, 2026. (Photo by Chief Mass Communication Specialist Darren M. Moore/U.S. Navy) The campaign for incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch strongly denied these rumors. The more-than-a-century-old law states that if a U.S. senator from Idaho resigns or dies within 30 days of the general election, then the governor could appoint a replacement and “no election for United States senator to fill said vacancy shall be held at such general election.” Risch is running against Todd Achilles, who has taken heat from from Risch’s campaign for running as an independent after serving in the Idaho Legislature as a Democrat. “This rumor is completely false,” Risch’s campaign manager Marc Kilmer told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email. “Jim Risch is leading in the polls. He is running an aggressive campaign. He will be victorious on November 3. This conspiracy theory is being perpetrated by our desperate opponent to take attention away from his liberal record. The only people who gamed the system this election were our opponent’s supporters who coerced Democrat David Roth to drop out and clear the field for Todd Achilles.” A spokesperson for the Achilles campaign denied the rumors started with the independent candidate’s campaign. “What’s concerning is that Jim Risch is pointing fingers instead of assuring voters that he won’t use the law in a way that would bypass the will of the voters,” Achilles’ Communication Director Crispin Gravatt wrote in an email. “He should clearly state that he will remain in the race through Election Day and, if elected, intends to serve the full 6-year term until he is 89 years old.” U.S. Senate candidate Democrat David Roth won his primary election in May, but withdrew from the race and removed his name from the ballot in September, citing a lack of support from his party. The Idaho Capital Sun reached out to the governor’s office for comment, but did not receive one. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE How are the other Idaho U.S. Senate candidates responding? At a candidate forum held Wednesday evening in Caldwell, Risch’s opponents addressed the possibility of the law being put to use. Risch wasn’t in attendance at Wednesday’s forum. “This has bubbled up recently. I don’t know if you guys have seen this,” moderator McKay Cunningham, a director of the master of applied public policy at College of Idaho, told candidates Wednesday. “Is this conspiracy theory? … What is the likelihood of this sort of thing happening? Maybe you haven’t even heard of it, but I’d like to get the candidates’ impressions on this question,” Cunningham said. In this file photo, Rep. Todd Achilles speaks from the House floor on the morning of March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Independents Achilles and Natalie Fleming, and Libertarian Matt Loesby, each said they thought the law’s use wouldn’t be well-met with Idaho voters. Most expressed doubt that it would be. “I think if it were tried, it would be challenged in courts, and it would be a whole big mess,” Loesby said. He said a more likely situation would be for Risch , who is 83, to retire after winning the election at some point into the six-year term. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Two days after a grand jury indicted a former Idaho state government employee on two felony counts of misuse of public funds, a local judge dismissed the case — after a request from the prosecutor. The case marked the first criminal charges — and a rare public update — to emerge from a yearslong investigation launched by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador that probed how the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare doled out $72 million in federal child care grants in 2021 and 2022. The official who was criminally charged, Ericka Rupp, oversaw the grant program. In the indictment, filed in Canyon County District Court last week, the grand jury charged Rupp with two felony counts of misuse of public funds and securities, for allegedly illegally authorizing, appropriating or otherwise misusing more than $300 of the government’s money. Boyd said he moved to drop the indictment based on feedback from jurors. “I, however, asked of them whether they felt the case was one worth pursuing in terms of resources,” Boyd wrote in a text message. “I truly wanted their opinion on this. They had spent several full days taking testimony. The majority of jurors felt my time was better spent focusing on the many other serious crimes they worked on.” For each count, the penalties could have been up to 14 years imprisonment and up to $10,000 in fines, according to state laws cited in the indictment. Rupp’s attorney, Scott McKay, declined to comment. In a Friday order, Third District Judge Thomas W. Whitney wrote he was dismissing the case upon the state’s request. The court hasn’t released records supporting the judge’s decision to dismiss the case. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Pending permission from the court, Boyd said he hopes to release a report with more details in the coming days. Asked whether he’d pursue charges against Rupp, or other people linked to the investigation, Boyd said: “The report should conclude my investigation.” The Idaho attorney general’s office could not immediately be reached for comment. Department of Health and Welfare spokesperson Greg Stahl directed questions about the case to parties involved. “(The Department of Health and Welfare) takes seriously its responsibility to be a good steward of taxpayer dollars and remains committed to transparency, accountability, and the appropriate use of public funds,” Stahl said in a statement. items.title: College sports is ‘living insanity.’ Politicians, of all people, are trying to stop the madness.
items.summary: Few things are bipartisan anymore, but on Monday, the U.S. Senate overwhelmingly agreed on a college athletics makeover. Jeramiah Dickey More money for student-athletes. Less money for agents. Fewer player transfers. Limits on conference realignment. Protections for the non-revenue Olympic sports that now exist — precariously — under the inescapable shadow of football. Would it all affect college
items.body: Few things are bipartisan anymore, but on Monday, the U.S. Senate overwhelmingly agreed on a college athletics makeover. Jeramiah Dickey More money for student-athletes. Less money for agents. Fewer player transfers. Limits on conference realignment. Protections for the non-revenue Olympic sports that now exist — precariously — under the inescapable shadow of football. Would it all affect college sports in Idaho? Absolutely. And should you care about all of that, even if you don’t care about college sports? Also, absolutely. An athletic program isn’t an entity unto itself. Increasingly, colleges and universities are looking to athletics as a revenue generator. This isn’t new: athletic success has long equated to increases in applications, enrollment and donor support. Now, colleges and universities want to use their athletic facilities to rake in revenue, and not just on game day. They want their facilities to bring in concerts and corporate retreats and support lucrative on-campus development. That long game hinges on staying competitive on turf and hardwood. Which puts college athletics in the unnatural position of hoping Congress will come to the rescue. “We’re living insanity, and the fact that the federal government’s having to get involved at all, I think, tells that story,” Boise State University athletic director Jeramiah Dickey told EdNews Thursday. What happened in Congress, and what happens next Monday’s 77-22 Senate vote was noteworthy — especially considering how much the sponsors crammed into the Protect College Sports Act . Far from a do-nothing bill, it tries to solve all of college sports’ problems in one shot. One big change: The bill will allow a college to pay its student-athletes up to $49 million a year, shattering the current $21 million “revenue sharing” cap. That higher cap would apply to everyone — but practically speaking, it may only be an issue in the NCAA’s so-called “Power Four” conferences, the Big Ten, the Southeastern Conference, the Big XII and the Atlantic Coast Conference. Terry Gawlik University of Idaho athletic director Terry Gawlik doesn’t expect to see her Big Sky Conference brethren bumping up against a $49 million cap. “They can make the cap as high as they want it for the Power Four, but we’re never going to get to that level of paying student athletes,” she said this week. “So that’s not something that affects us daily.” But the $49 million cap could affect Boise State. The Broncos made the first 12-team College Football Playoff two years ago and are contenders again this year — and landing in the CFP will pit Boise State against big-money programs that could push up to the salary cap. (Boise State paid its student-athletes $10 million last budget year.) Dickey said he’s “not a huge fan” of the $49 million cap, but he’s glad to see the bill set some kind of maximum. Both Gawlik and Dickey like another key piece of the bill. It would allow student-athletes to transfer once in their college careers — and force repeat transfers to sit out a season. The limits on transfers will restore stability in the locker room, Gawlik said. In a related vein, Dickey likes the limited, five-year window for athletes to complete their playing careers. “This is a chapter,” he said. “This is not forever.” The bill also sidesteps a political minefield: state laws restricting transgender athletes. As Politico reported last month , co-sponsor Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, inserted language clarifying that the federal law would not supersede state bans on transgender athletes. For Gov. Brad Little, who signed the nation’s first transgender athletics ban into law in 2020 , that’s a non-negotiable, spokeswoman Emily Callihan said this week. “Gov. IEA is
items.body: The Idaho Education Association (IEA) is cutting about 13% of its staff and closing its regional offices, leaders of the statewide teachers’ union announced this week. The cost-cutting measures come after union members told IEA’s board of directors to take a closer look at the organization’s budget and after a new law restricting taxpayer support for teachers’ union activities took effect. IEA is eliminating four union organizer positions, according to Executive Director Paul Stark. It’s also closing five regional offices, “centralizing operations in its Boise office.” And it’s turning Summer Institute, an annual professional development event, into an every-other-year event. IEA’s board of directors announced the cuts in an email to union members Monday. The board includes two dozen people, most of whom represent nine different geographic regions of the state. “Over the summer, we, your elected Board of Directors, carefully considered several options, asked difficult questions, and made decisions to put IEA on stronger financial footing for the future,” the board’s email said. “These decisions were not made lightly. They affect people. People who have dedicated themselves to serving our members and our profession.” Paul Stark, executive director of the Idaho Education Association " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-701x1180.jpg" class="wp-image-44392 size-thumbnail" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-119x200.jpg" alt="" width="119" height="200" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-119x200.jpg 119w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-368x620.jpg 368w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-701x1180.jpg 701w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-913x1536.jpg 913w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-1217x2048.jpg 1217w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-scaled.jpg 1521w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 119px) 100vw, 119px" /> Paul Stark, executive director of the Idaho Education Association The cuts followed a directive from IEA’s Delegate Assembly, a gathering of hundreds of local union leaders, the email said. In April the assembly told the board to “thoroughly examine” IEA’s budget and ensure that the union was “operating within its means.” The board also considered “the challenges created by recent legislative policies, including House Bill 516 ,” the email said. Enacted during this year’s legislative session , House Bill 516 prohibited public schools from using taxpayer-funded resources, such as payroll systems, to accommodate union activities. The Delegate Assembly issued a vote of no confidence in Gov. Brad Little for signing the “union-busting” bill into law. It took effect July 1. It’s unclear to what extent HB 516 factored into the downsizing. Among other restrictions, the law prohibits school districts from using payroll systems to deduct union dues. Districts also can’t offer teachers paid time off to engage in union activities unless IEA reimburses the district. And districts can’t give the union teachers’ contact information without their consent. The Freedom Foundation — an anti-union think tank based in Olympia, Wash. — for years lobbied lawmakers to enact the restrictions after it published a report arguing that Idaho unions were benefiting from government funds, facilities, resources and personnel. IEA leaders have repeatedly said that the union doesn’t receive taxpayer funding. But Stark didn’t provide specifics on how the law factored into the layoffs and office closures. “Idaho students and educators are only one month into the new school year, so the full effects of HB 516 on public education and the IEA have yet to be seen,” he said in an emailed statement Wednesday.

Critchfield, a Republican, had originally agreed to an Oct. 12 debate against Democratic nominee Becky Sundin Mitchell, sponsored by KTVB. Critchfield now says she will not appear unless a third-party candidate — Constitution Party nominee Teresa Roundy — is also on the stage. The news comes
items.body: A televised state superintendent’s debate is off, after incumbent Debbie Critchfield backed out this week. Critchfield, a Republican, had originally agreed to an Oct. 12 debate against Democratic nominee Becky Sundin Mitchell, sponsored by KTVB. Critchfield now says she will not appear unless a third-party candidate — Constitution Party nominee Teresa Roundy — is also on the stage. The news comes barely a week after Critchfield and Sundin Mitchell appeared at a debate co-sponsored by Idaho EdNews and The College of Idaho . Roundy did not qualify for the Sept. 22 debate, since her campaign did not meet the co-sponsors’ fundraising threshold. The KTVB debate had a similar fundraising threshold, one the station says it has had in place for decades . Roundy’s campaign has not raised or spent any money, according to Idaho sunshine reports. In a statement to KTVB, Critchfield said her decision “isn’t about avoiding a debate,” but is instead about respecting the voters and the process. “There are three candidates in this race, and I believe voters deserve the opportunity to hear from all three,” Critchfield said in a statement to KTVB. “It’s not my place — or anyone else’s — to decide for voters which candidates are viable enough to be heard.” In a statement, Sundin Mitchell said Critchfield should be willing to answer questions about her record. “KTVB set its criteria for participation, and her decision to withdraw means Idaho voters will no longer get the opportunity to hear the candidates answer questions side by side,” Sundin Mitchell said. “Debates matter because elected officials should be willing to defend their records directly to the people they serve.” With the KTVB debate cancelled, Critchfield and Sundin Mitchell will probably not square off again before the Nov. 3 general election. The candidates have no other debates scheduled in the remaining five weeks of the campaign. The cancellation continues what has become an election-year trend. Debates between statewide candidates, once commonplace, have been nearly nonexistent this fall. Several Republican incumbents have refused to debate their opponents — rejecting or ignoring invitations to joint events. Gov. Brad Little, U.S. Sen. Jim Risch and Attorney General Raúl Labrador are unlikely to debate their opponents before the election. Consequently, the League of Women Voters has instead sponsored open forums, not debates, for whichever candidates decide to attend. An Oct. 6 Boise forum will feature Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens and independent candidate John Stegner; Little has not responded to the invitation. More coverage: Watch our Sept. 22 state superintendent’s debate in full, read our coverage from the debate , and read an in-depth analysis on the demise of debates in Idaho .

items.body: State Rep. Steve Berch, D-Boise, asks a question during the March 16, 2026, Idaho House Local Government Committee meeting at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) An incumbent Boise state representative who lives in a competitive legislative district has raised the most money of any candidate for the Idaho Legislature in 2026, online state campaign finance records show. Rep. Steve Berch, D-Boise, has raised $212,580.79 as of Tuesday afternoon. Although Republicans control a supermajority in the Idaho Legislature, Berch is the only candidate in Idaho’s 105 legislative districts who has raised more than $200,000 this year. Search Idaho campaign finance records online To search through finance records for each Idaho candidate, go to Idaho Sunshine, the Idaho Secretary of State’s campaign finance website . Through Idaho Sunshine, the public can search for candidates, political action committees, campaign expenditures, campaign contributions, reports and more. Berch also raised the most money heading into this year’s primary elections , the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. In an interview Tuesday, Berch attributed his fundraising success to engaging directly with voters and knocking on tens of thousands of doors in his legislative district. “It’s really very humbling, and it tells me that people like what I’m doing in terms of knocking on doors, holding in-person town hall meetings and sending out very detailed newsletters so they know the reason why I vote the way I do,” Berch said. Most of Berch’s campaign contributions came from people and from within Idaho. According to online state campaign finance reports, Berch raised $153,816 from people, $27,450 from companies, $9,000 from political committees and $1,000 from Democratic central committees. Berch raised $169,226 in Idaho and $22,040 from out-of-state donors, records show. The rest of Berch’s campaign money was un-itemized. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More Berch represents District 15 in west Boise, which has flipped back and forth between Democratic and Republican control since at least 2018. Berch’s opponent in the Nov. 3 general election, Republican Steve Keyser, has reported raising $13,592.67. District 15 is one of the rare truly split legislative districts in Idaho. For the past two years, Berch held one of the legislative seats in District 15 while Republicans held the other two. Two years before, Berch and the Democrats controlled two of the district’s seats while Republicans held just one. For that reason, both Republicans and Democrats will be looking to pick up a seat in District 15 in November’s general election What other Idaho legislative candidates are raising the most money Among the 10 Idaho legislative candidates who raised the most campaign money in 2026, seven are Republicans and three are Democrats. In total, six candidates have reported raising more than $100,000 in campaign money this year. Although it was decided months ago, Idaho’s primary election appears to have played a big role in campaign fundraising this year. Two candidates from the Republican primary election for Idaho Senate District 1, Sen. Jim Woodward and former Sen. Scott Herndon, were among the top four legislative candidates in terms of campaign fundraising for 2026. Herndon won the primary in May and advanced to the Nov. 3 general election, where he is running against independent candidate Steve Johnson. Legislative leadership positions also may have played a role in campaign fundraising this year. The League of Women Voters and Caldwell chamber hosted a U.S. Senate candidate forum
items.body: From left, League of Women Voters of Idaho President Jean Henscheid, independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles, College of Idaho moderatorsLatonia Haney Keith and McKay Cunningham, Libertarian Matt Loesby, center, independent Natalie Fleming, and Caldwell Chamber of Commerce Executive Director Travis Palmer. The League of Women Voters and Caldwell chamber hosted a U.S. Senate candidate forum Sept. 30 at Caldwell City Hall. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Three out of four candidates running to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate discussed their differing approaches on tariffs, military actions, immigration, and more Wednesday night in Caldwell. The race’s incumbent, Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, declined to participate. Independents Todd Achilles and Natalie Fleming, and Libertarian Matt Loesby, spoke at the forum hosted by the League of Women Voters, Caldwell Chamber of Commerce and the local American Association of University Women at Caldwell City Hall. 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More The three candidates differed in their proposals to address the federal budget deficit, reform immigration, and rein in military action abroad. Risch’s campaign manager Marc Kilmer told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email that Risch didn’t participate because, “It was organized by someone who has publicly endorsed our opponent, and therefore we felt it would not be an impartial debate.” Kilmer said the endorsement came from former Idaho Republican state Rep. Julie Yamamoto of Caldwell, but it wasn’t clear how she was connected to the organizers. He couldn’t immediately be reached to clarify. League of Women Voters of Idaho President Jean Henscheid told the Sun she didn’t know of any organizers that endorsed a candidate in the race. To watch the entire forum, visit the City of Caldwell Youtube page . How would the candidates address the high cost of living and tariffs? All of the candidates agreed that the existing 50% tariff on a range of Canadian good s, should be rolled back and implemented more strategically. Achilles argued that Congress needed to “take back control” of tariff policy from the White House, and manage them in a “more strategic way” to protect domestic industries. “Congress needs to stand up and be an independent branch of government, and execute their constitutional duties, which is to be in control of tariffs,” he said. Loesby argued that tariffs were a small part of the problem when it came to addressing high costs of living for Americans. He agreed that the existing high tariffs should be rolled back and the taxes on imported products should be used to address trade imbalances with China. To address cost of living challenges, he said the U.S. needed to “end all these horrific foreign wars,” and “deport the millions of people who should not be in our country” to address housing costs. items.body: With help from the Legislature, Idaho’s largest school district has the lowest property tax rate in the state and can build two new buildings over the next year without increasing its local tax burden. At a time when bonds and levies are hard to pass, West Ada School District trustees on Monday night approved a complicated loan agreement that will give the district $56.4 million in cash. The money will help the district turn a vacant warehouse into a career and technical education center on Locust Grove and rebuild Lake Hazel Elementary, with both projects expected to open in fall 2027. The district will pay the loan off over 15 years with ongoing state facilities funding. West Ada CFO Dave Roberts said the district expects at least $35.8 million in sales tax every year from House Bill 292 , passed in 2023. The bill was designed to reduce school districts’ property tax burden. A fraction of that annual appropriation, $5.3 million, will pay off the loan without increasing property taxes. “It’s possible that with this type of funding that West Ada may be able to build buildings without ever going to taxpayers again,” Roberts told EdNews on Tuesday. The projects follow the district’s recent completion of Independence Elementary in Star, which was built with state modernization funds from House Bill 521 and without an increase in property taxes. In a student survey last fall, 46% of Notus junior high school and high school students listed mental health as a concern. District Superintendent Jen Wright thought she had found a partial solution. She wanted to use $60,000 in federal grants to hire a behavioral health coordinator for preschool through 12 th grade. But last week, legislators tabled the program, leaving Notus and nine other rural schools shut out on funding. “I was really thinking that we were going to get it,” Wright said in an interview Tuesday. “It’s just very disappointing.” Until last week, the Department of Health and Welfare was pursuing a $1.2 million behavioral health hub program — designed to offer optional in-person or telehealth services to students and families. The money was going to come from a fraction of Idaho’s $186 million federal rural healthcare transformation grant . The Legislature’s Rural Health Transformation Committee abruptly put the behavioral health hub proposal on hold Friday — shifting the $1.2 million out of the program. Committee members noted that the Legislature had rejected a similar proposal in 2024 . Before Friday’s vote, nine districts had applied for behavioral health grants: Aberdeen, American Falls, Cascade, Castleford, Garden Valley, Marsing, Notus, Snake River and Wilder. Heritage Academy Public Charter in Jerome also applied. All the applicants were rural — and some distance from the closest clinic. In Notus’ case, the nearest mental health services are in Caldwell, a half hour drive away. Aberdeen School District Superintendent Scott Muir was hoping to use a $110,000 grant to bridge the gap between his rural community and health services in American Falls, about 20 minutes away, and Pocatello, about 50 minutes away. The grant would have gone toward new mental health and wellness services, additional counseling support and facilities upgrades. “We believe these efforts would have had a meaningful impact on the overall well-being of our students and community,” Muir said in an email to EdNews Tuesday. Friday’s committee vote came as a surprise to Wright. She said she only learned Notus had lost out on its grant through EdNews’ coverage of the hearing. The sudden news means Notus will look for other options. A new partnership with Insight Counseling — a third party that already works with Marsing and Wilder — will provide Notus with a clinical counselor. items.body: Idaho showed a 66% rise of 18 and 19-year-old registered voters between 2018 and 2022. Then, in 2023, Idaho legislators passed new voting laws targeted at student voters. After the laws took effect, Idaho saw a 23% decline in 18- and 19-year-old registered voters. Idaho is now last in the nation in the percentage of 18-year-old registered voters compared to registered voters aged 45 and older. Despite zero evidence of Idaho students fraudulently using their student IDs to vote, the law removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification. Previously, students could use their ID as a form of identification for registering to vote, and to vote on election day. BABE VOTE and the League of Women Voters of Idaho challenged the laws in court. However, our case was dismissed without a trial. If granted a trial, we would have shown evidence of legally eligible Idaho voters who were unable to vote under the new laws. Upon pushback from the community, Representative Brent Crane (R-Nampa) who helped pass the laws, said,“[the laws] were doing exactly what they were designed to do.” We continue to hear positive messages from our Secretary of State about how easy it is for Idahoans to register and vote. But for some legally eligible Idahoans, it has not been easy. Although these laws specifically targeted students, they have created barriers for other Idahoans—including people who have moved, changed their names, or no longer drive. Sam Sandmire, a BABE VOTE member, spent more than an hour on the phone with the Secretary of State’s staff troubleshooting the system as she tried to change her address on her voter registration. It took her more than a week and additional phone calls before she was able to request an absentee ballot. This is not a one-time occurrence. Many long-time voters have reported that they have been removed from the voter database, even though they have voted consistently in recent elections. So these are not hypothetical concerns. They are issues we are hearing about and experiencing ourselves. If voters are unaware of potential problems or delays, they may wait until it is too late to resolve them. BABE VOTE does not want to discourage anyone from registering or voting. Our goal is to warn legally eligible voters to start now: check your voter registration, register or re-register to vote, and make a plan to vote, whether by absentee ballot, early in person, or at the polls on Election Day. Idahoans should not have to navigate unnecessary obstacles to exercise their right to vote, but until those obstacles are addressed, voters need to know they exist. Voting should not be a last-minute scramble. Don’t wait until Election Day. Check your registration, make a plan, and give yourself time to resolve any problems so you can cast your ballot. Babe, VOTE! BABE VOTE is a non-partisan, non-profit that empowers young people to organize their communities for democracy.

items.body: The Senate has overwhelmingly endorsed a far-reaching and bipartisan bill to overhaul college sports. Idaho Republican Sens. Mike Crapo and Jim Risch both voted for the Protect College Sports Act of 2026 , which passed Monday on a 77-22 vote . The bill still allows “revenue sharing,” direct payments to athletes. The spending cap would increase from $21.5 million to roughly $49 million, ESPN reported . Other provisions of the bill would allow student-athletes to transfer only once in their college careers; cap fees to agents at 5%; and restrict colleges and universities from cutting programs in Olympic sports in order to sink the savings into football. “College athletics are facing significant challenges Congress can and must meaningfully address,” Crapo said in a news release Tuesday. “The Protect College Sports Act provides much-needed clarity and consistency for student athletes and higher education institutions.” In the same news release, Idaho’s three university presidents took turns hailing the bill. “The Protect College Sports Act is an important pathway for creating a stable, fair foundation for college athletics,” Boise State University President David Hahn said. Despite the overwhelming Senate vote — and backing from President Donald Trump — the Protect College Sports Act is not a done deal. It still needs to pass the House, which is on recess until after the November election. If the House fails to act on the bill during a lame-duck session after the elections, ESPN noted, the process would have to start over in the next congressional session. (Shelby Wyatt/Source NM) An Idaho judge dismissed a lawsuit from a Boise daycare and parents that sought to block enforcement of a state law that bans daycares from requiring vaccines or medical treatment. The lawsuit claimed that the Idaho Medical Freedom Act was unconstitutionally vague, arguing its language bans a range of routine health protections — including handwashing and sending home sick kids. But last week, Chief U.S. District Judge for the District of Idaho Amanda K. Brailsford granted Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador’s request to dismiss the lawsuit, which was brought by Le Soleil Child Care LLC, and three parents whose kids attend the daycare or hope to. In her ruling, the federal judge wrote she agreed with Labrador’s interpretation of the law’s definition of “medical interventions,” writing that they refer to health actions that are “medical in nature.” “The (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) plainly and unambiguously sets out a standard of prohibited conduct that gives a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is prohibited,” Brailsford wrote, ruling that the daycare didn’t show that the state law was unconstitutionally vague. “The Court agrees with the AG that Le Soleil is free to promote its beliefs and values about public health and vaccinations …” the judge wrote. “The only thing the (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) prevents is Le Soleil requiring that only vaccinated students hear those values.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. A daycare does not,” Labrador said in a statement . “The Legislature protected that choice in the Medical Freedom Act, and the court upheld it. (Photo by Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle) A new data center campus could soon be coming to federal land near Hermiston in eastern Oregon. It would be the first in Oregon sited on federal public land, and one of at least 12 proposed for more than 17,500 Bureau of Land Management acres across western states under President Donald Trump’s July 2025 executive order to hasten data center development. The proposals on federal land in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming were first reported last week by The Washington Sun, whose reporters reviewed difficult to find right-of-way requests via BLM’s Mineral and Land Records System . The bulk of federally managed land in the U.S. is in the West, including in Oregon where half the state’s land is owned and managed by the federal government. Oregon is among the top 10 markets for data centers in the U.S., according to Pew Research. Under the executive order, Trump mandated that federally owned land and resources be used for “the expeditious and orderly development of data centers (…) to be used in service of the prosperity and security of the American people.” It’s the first time the Bureau of Land Management, tasked with managing more than 245 million public acres for uses that include animal grazing, timber harvesting and recreation, has been ordered to include data centers in its portfolio. Several months after Trump issued the order, the California-based energy company Copia, which has an office in Lake Oswego, submitted an application to site the Charlestown Data Center and Battery Energy Storage System in Umatilla County on 106 acres of BLM land. The company most recently submitted a draft plan for development of the data center project on May 8, 2026, available only via federal public records request, according to Sarah Bennett, a spokesperson for the bureau’s Northwest region office. items.body: An independent conservative running in a swing district against a Republican incumbent and a Democratic challenger means anything could happen in November. Rep. Mike Pohanka, R-Jerome, narrowly won the 2024 general election over Democrat Ned Burns by 2.4 percentage points. Pohanka now faces a three-way race against a Democrat with a long career in education and a Christian conservative independent who believes the government has turned away from God. Pohanka is seeking a second term in District 26 House Seat A. District 26 includes blue voters in Blaine County and red voters to the south in Jerome and Lincoln counties. But Pohanka said he considers himself colorblind. He said he’s a public servant who wants to help his constituents. “I have people coming up to me saying, ‘You know what? I’m a Democrat, and I’m voting for you because you are a person that cares and you’re doing the job,'” Pohanka said. That attitude encouraged independent Bella Schiffler to run. She interned for two lawmakers in Boise and said she learned that many politicians who call themselves conservative aren’t really conservative. Schiffler said education has become “woke,” citing a debunked hoax about litter boxes in schools. She told EdNews that she would be in favor of taking away women’s right to vote if it helped the country move closer to God. “America is a Christian nation, and we are founded on godly principles,” Schiffler said. Pohanka said he hopes Schiffler will not split the conservative vote in November, which happened two years ago when her aunt, Kala Tate, ran for the Senate as an independent. Anita Janis, chair of the Jerome County Democrats, wants to bring her experiences of teaching around the country to the Legislature. She said Idaho can learn from other states, where education funding works differently. “I have lived in other states where there would never be a levy put together to support salaries,” Janis said. She wants to see the Legislature fulfill its duty under the Idaho Constitution to fund public schools. Election Day is Nov. 3. But on Friday, lawmakers slammed the brakes on those applications and the $1.2 million program. The Rural Health Transformation Committee put the behavioral health hubs on hold — at least until the 2027 legislative session, which begins in January. Committee members said the hub proposal represents a policy change and lawmakers should have the chance to vote on it. The $1.2 million is a small part of Idaho’s $186 million rural health bank account — Phase One of a five-year, federally funded grant program . But Friday’s committee discussion underscores a bigger debate over the funds. The Department of Health and Welfare is racing to commit the $186 million by the feds’ Oct. 30 deadline. But legislators have wanted oversight over the spending — creating the eight-member House-Senate rural health committee for that purpose. Sen. items.body: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright (center) visits Idaho National Laboratory with Idaho Gov. Brad Little (right) in December 2025. (Photo courtesy of Sarah Wood/U.S. Department of Energy) Editor’s Note: This is the first installment of a three-part Idaho Capital Sun series examining the proposal to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Part one focuses on Gov. Brad Little’s role in negotiations and his priorities for Idaho. The series continues Monday and Tuesday with a closer look at the cases for and against bringing a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Idaho Gov. Brad Little said he will not jeopardize the health of the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer or the health of Idahoans as he continues to negotiate potentially bringing a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. “I’ve had this direct conversation with Secretary (of Energy Chris) Wright: Disposal of spent fuel over the aquifer in Idaho – that’s a nonstarter,” Little said in an interview Wednesday at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. In July, U.S. Department of Energy officials announced that Idaho is one of five states selected as a finalist to host one of the new innovation campuses. Little signed a memorandum of understanding in July with the U.S. Department of Energy, or DOE, to hold formal discussions and negotiations about bringing an innovation campus to Idaho. The Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer is outlined in orange of this map of Washington, Oregon and Idaho. (Map courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey) If Idaho is selected as a host site, the federal government has said the state will have to accept shipments of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste from other states. A Request for Information Response that Little signed and submitted to the federal government in March describes an accelerated process that takes “months rather than decades” to bring the “initial capabilities” of a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus online in 2027. But on Wednesday, Little said things aren’t moving that quickly. “There’s a long way to go before this happens,” Little said. “(The DOE) would love to identify some sites, and I believe … they may need something by the end of the year. But it will not be in any way, shape or form a final agreement.” Little said the documents he signed do not obligate Idaho to host an innovation campus or accept nuclear fuel or radioactive waste. Instead, the agreements simply bring Idaho to the negotiating table, the governor said. Little said it makes sense for Idaho to be at the negotiating table because of the potential economic benefits to the state, the infrastructure, the experience at Idaho National Laboratory in eastern Idaho and the need for additional, reliable energy. The memorandum of understanding lists a Sept. 30 deadline, but Little said he doesn’t think agreements will be reached that quickly, and he suggested the two sides could either continue talks or sign another memorandum of understanding with a later deadline. Officials at Idaho National Laboratory declined to comment for this series of articles. What is a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus? items.body: West Ada Education Services Director David Reinhart couldn’t get through a presentation to some 150 parents, teachers and community members without being shouted at Tuesday night. Interruptions from the crowd were occasionally met with applause or boos. Emotions were high: In November, district leaders will decide whether to close the district’s McMillan Elementary. Tuesday’s meeting was held to inform families and invite input. Reinhart persisted through the interruptions, sharing numbers through a projector above his head in the school’s gymnasium. It was the second such meeting at the school, but drew about 100 more attendees. The first meeting, on Sept. 16, drew about 50 people, KTVB reported. A school is more than just numbers, Reinhart said. But McMillan Elementary’s enrollment is shrinking, with nearly 300 empty seats. It needs around $5.5 million in repairs. Declining enrollment and pricey repair bills have led West Ada trustees to consider closing the school. Parents and teachers like the school. Class sizes hover around 19 students. Teachers say they know students by name and often remember them long after they move on to middle school. Still, declining enrollment prompted West Ada administrators to ask trustees to take a scrutinizing look at the school’s future. “T he decline in enrollment has been sharp, so we want to make good use of our resources, and that’s why we brought it to their attention,” Reinhart told parents. Earlier this month, Reinhart presented the possibility of closing McMillan to the board after the district’s long-range planning committee — made up of parents from across the district — recommended the board consider closing the school. “T hey had a general concern that empty rooms cost taxpayers extra money,” Reinhart said. items.body: The Boise School District says it could close a number of schools, convert others, and revamp which grades attend high school and junior high as it faces declining enrollment. The district rolled out a number of proposals during virtual and in-person meetings this week it called “The Future of Boise Schools.” Meeting invitations didn’t hint at the scale of the proposed changes, but did note that final decisions have not been made. The proposals include shutting down or combining some grade schools, closing several junior high schools, moving high schools from three years to four, and possibly adding a specialized new high school. Declining enrollment Tracy Richter, a consultant, works with school districts across the country, which all face the same issue. “We don’t have a district that we’re working with anywhere in the country that is rising in enrollment,” Richter said, which he attributed to a decline in birth rates across the country. Factors like housing availability are also affecting school district enrollment — families may be holding onto homes longer, even after children have grown up and moved out, and young families may struggle to afford the homes that are available. When costs are prohibitive for young families to move in, it does not lead to more students for the district, Richter said. The housing market, Richter said, creates another barrier for families looking to move. “Nobody wants to go to half the house for twice the money and four times the interest rate.” Richter works for HPM, a consulting company contracted by the Boise School District to create a Long-Range Facilities Master Plan. The Boise School District currently has 9,000 open seats, 5,000 of which are at the elementary school level. Part of the plan aims to propose solutions to declining student enrollment, which is creating excess capacity, particularly at the district’s elementary and junior high schools. To do so, HPM has developed and is seeking public feedback on three potential scenarios: addressing excess capacity at the high school level, junior high level, or elementary school level. The company also developed “concepts,” or ways to implement each scenario, including closing some elementary schools in the district, moving 9th grade from the junior high to high school level, and changing enrollment areas and boundaries for schools. Richter presented each of the scenarios at a virtual and in-person meetings this week. District patrons are being encouraged to review the potential scenarios and concepts and submit their feedback via a Fall Community Survey , available on the district’s master planning webpage . Richter said that his team received 900 responses from an initial survey in the spring, which helped them develop the scenarios under consideration now. Richter anticipated it would take until February or March to develop a facilities master plan and make a recommendation that the district’s board of trustees would then adopt. “What we want people to understand is that we’re not even close to any recommendations yet,” Richter said, “and we want to make sure that we are doing as transparent of a process as we can to make sure we’re getting as much input as we can from the community.” The district could make decisions on any potential funding needed to implement the changes, such as bonds, after the master plan is established, Richter said. He estimated it could take two to five years for the district to implement any recommendation. items.body: Two Idaho colleges landed notable spots in U.S. News & World Report’s latest annual college rankings . The University of Idaho received a lofty national ranking for affordability, while a Moscow-based college — connected to a controversial church with ties to Christian nationalism — is Idaho’s highest-ranked liberal arts college. College and university leaders closely watch the annual rankings — and on Tuesday, the U of I and Lewis-Clark State College were quick to send out news releases touting their numbers. U.S. News & World Report uses more than 15 metrics for its overall college and university rankings. Student outcomes — graduation and retention rates and post-graduation earnings — account for 52% of the overall score. The magazine then sorts colleges and universities into several separate classifications. Here are some takeaways (with links to the full reports for each school): University of Idaho The U of I received the state’s top grade in the national universities category, receiving a middle-of-the-pack No. 208 ranking. U.S. News & World Report ranked 427 national universities. The U of I ranked highest on the list of “best value schools,” coming in No. 23 overall. The U of I is the highest-ranked public university in this category. For the past several years, the U of I has trailed only one other public institution, the University of North Carolina. “This ranking reflects what we work hard to deliver every day: an exceptional education that remains within reach for students and families,” U of I President Scott Green said in a news release. “Our students pursue research, learn by doing and build connections that prepare them to succeed after graduation, creating value not just for Idaho but nationally as well through the work they go on to do.” The U of I also ranked No. 66 as a best value school for in-state students. Boise State University Boise State ranked No. 299 in the national universities category. Its top-ranked program, nursing, came in at No. 94. Idaho State University Idaho State landed between No. 382 and No. 422 among national universities (no specific ranking was released). Idaho State’s highest-ranked program, also in nursing, came in at No. 135. Lewis-Clark State College LC State ranked No. 27 among 73 regional colleges in the West. LC State was also ranked No. 6 among public schools, climbing two spots from last year. The college also landed No. 23 for social mobility — which measures success rates for Pell Grant recipients — and climbed 12 spots in this category. In a news release, LC State noted that it is the only Top 10 public college in Idaho or Washington. “LC State continues to enhance the incredible value it provides to students, families, communities, and Idaho, and we’re grateful that this ranking captures that progression,” President Cynthia Pemberton said. Northwest Nazarene University NNU ranked No. 41 among 110 regional universities in the West. It ranked No. 19 among private schools, and No. 71 for social mobility. New Saint Andrews College New Saint Andrews ranked No. 132 among 206 national liberal arts colleges, and No. 121 among private schools. Doug Wilson — pastor of Moscow-based Christ Church — founded New Saint Andrews in 1994 and is a permanent member of the college’s board. (Click here for a 2024 Boise State Public Radio podcast series on Christian nationalism, with segments focused on Christ Church and Wilson.) The College of Idaho C of I ranked No. 142 among national liberal arts colleges, and No. 128 among private schools. Brigham Young University-Idaho BYU-Idaho, owned by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, ranked No. 172 among national liberal arts colleges, and No. 148 among private schools. Its undergraduate engineering program ranked No. 71.

items.body: CALDWELL — It was a refreshing night on the campaign trail Tuesday. And that’s exactly the problem. It’s unusual — make that rare — to see two statewide candidates on the same stage. Facing a live audience of voters. Answering actual questions. Talking in detail about priorities and policies. Two candidates, to their credit, taking their case to the people. I wish I could say Tuesday night’s debate between GOP state superintendent Debbie Critchfield and Democratic challenger Becky Sundin Mitchell was just the start of a robust fall debate season. That, unfortunately, wouldn’t be honest. See for yourself. Click here to watch Tuesday’s debate. The fact is that Tuesday’s debate — co-sponsored by Idaho EdNews and The College of Idaho — is the exception to the rule. Critchfield and Sundin Mitchell will appear again at an Oct. 12 debate sponsored by KTVB in Boise. Aside from that, it’s quiet out there. Way too quiet. Other Republican incumbents aren’t debating. Gov. Brad Little, Sen. Jim Risch and Attorney General Raúl Labrador either turned down or ignored invites from KTVB. What gives? In the spirit of the election season — and the spirit of helping you make an informed choice — pick your favorite sports metaphor. Marc Johnson, a longtime fixture in former Gov. Cecil Andrus’ inner circle, recently invoked the name of legendary North Carolina basketball coach Dean Smith. Johnson — who seldom passes up the chance to chide Idaho Republicans in general, and Risch in particular — accused Idaho’s junior senator of cribbing Smith’s “four-corners” offense . When Smith’s teams had what appeared to be an insurmountable lead, he’d spread players on the four corners of the front court, directing them to pass the ball around with no intention of taking a shot or doing, well, anything. An annoying but maddeningly effective way to run out the clock. Not to try to upstage Johnson, I’ll call the no-debate gameplan a “business decision.” In football, when a player sidesteps a hit from an opposing player, usually a bigger one moving at full speed, that’s a business decision. Avoid a potential injury — or, at least, some short-term pain — and protect your future earnings potential. Call bailing on debates whatever you want. Just don’t call it gutsy. And their opponents, standing on the sidelines, have little left to do but grumble. At a town hall meeting in Boise last week, independent gubernatorial candidate John Stegner was asked whether he’d get the chance at a debate. He said he wasn’t counting on it. “(It’s) disconcerting at best (and) disheartening at worst,” said Stegner, picking his words with the deliberation befitting a former state Supreme Court justice. Independent Senate candidate Todd Achilles got some social media traffic and some news coverage recently, by recording a brief and awkward Boise Airport exchange with Risch . Achilles tried to get Risch to commit to a debate. Risch walked away; at the end of the video, Risch is seen talking to airport security. Achilles tried to keep the narrative going in a campaign text a few days later. “Todd again,” the text began. “Risch still has not said a word since he pulled his hand away and kept walking.” Democratic challenger Becky Sundin Mitchell, right, and Republican incumbent Debbie Critchfield participate in a debate for Idaho Superintendent of Public Instruction on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, at the College of Idaho in Caldwell. To his right are retired founder of the Idaho Innocence Project Greg Hampikian and The Innocence Center Executive Director Mike Semanchik. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Correction: This story was corrected at 2:08 p.m. on Sept. 24 to clarify the Idaho Innocence Project’s role in Charles Fain’s case. The Idaho Innocence Project helped secure Fain’s certificate of innocence and identify the true perpetrator, but was not involved in his original exoneration. Charles Fain says his three favorite letters in the alphabet are D-N-A. In 2001, Fain was exonerated and released from an Idaho prison after nearly 20 years on death row for a rape and murder he did not commit, using DNA analysis. After his release, the Idaho Innocence Project helped police identify the true perpetrator and got Fain a certificate of innocence and compensation for wrongful conviction. The Idaho Innocence Project has been shuttered for more than two years because of a lack of funding. However, on Sept. 17, Fain joined Innocence Project founder Greg Hampikian and fellow exoneree Amanda Knox to usher in a new group continuing the work of overturning wrongful convictions. The Innocence Center board member and exoneree Amanda Knox and retired founder of the Idaho Innocence Project Greg Hampikian. Hampikian lent his DNA expertise to Knox’s defense team to help free her from an Italian prison. (Photo by G Kenny3 Photography) Knox sits on the board of The Innocence Center , a nonprofit, free law firm based in San Diego that will take on cases in Idaho to try and free wrongfully convicted inmates. Hampikian, a forensic DNA expert, also lent his expertise to Knox’s defense team in the highly publicized case and helped free her from an Italian prison after she was wrongfully sentenced for the murder of her roommate while studying abroad. “It would be a desperate situation if these projects didn’t exist,” Knox said in an interview last week in Boise. “And when I heard that the Idaho Innocence Project was shutting down, I was really, really worried for the state of Idaho, because who else is going to do it?” The Innocence Center Executive Director Mike Semanchik was admitted to the Idaho bar on Sept. 18 so that he may work as an attorney for these cases in Idaho. “We’re committed to making this happen and making sure that wherever there are innocent people in prison, there’s an organization to support them,” Semanchik told a small gathering last week to kickoff the new work. Hampikian said he personally selected The Innocence Center to take up the work. “My last great act, after 20 years of the Innocence Project, was to choose a successor,” Hampikian said. “… (Semanchik) said, ‘I’ll get barred in Idaho, and I’ll take the cases until we raise the money.’ And I was like, ‘Oh, this guy’s got skin in the game.’” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: The Idaho Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force meets on Sept. 23, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) A group of rural Idaho hospital leaders, state officials and tribal representatives met for the first time Wednesday to oversee the process of awarding nearly $190 million in federal rural health grants. The Idaho Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force received an update on the state’s administration of the federal Rural Health Transformation grant program — a nationwide $50 billion, five-year federal grant Congress approved through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year. Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare) “We are building and flying the plane at the same time. That feels like it’s been the consistent theme of this,” Idaho Department Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron said Wednesday. The task force is meant to provide input on the process of implementation, help navigate potential challenges, and ensure the state is balancing statewide initiatives with actual needs of rural communities, Charron said. The nearly 20 funding opportunities posted by the state have closed, and Health and Welfare staff are reviewing applications to award subgrants. The opportunities include funding to provide school-based family support, chronic disease prevention and cancer screening, a cognitive care network, and diabetes prevention and management. The agency awarded national nonprofit Comagine Health with a grant to create a collaborative system to improve maternal and child health statewide, according to the program website. The state is nearing an Oct. 30 deadline to award all of the $186 million received for the first year of the program. “It is going to be a very, very tight timeline coming up to the end,” Charron said. For a health provider infrastructure opportunity, which will be about $97 million of the total grant, Charron said the agency received more than 250 applications asking for a total of more than $300 million. “That means that we will have to say no to some,” she said. Idaho submitted its first required report to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid, which is overseeing the program, on Aug. 31. The report will help determine how much funding the state gets in the second year of the five-year program. Charron said that the state hasn’t heard feedback on that report yet. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho’s received sightly less funding because of low rural population density When Congress approved the funding, it split the $50 billion into two allocation methods. Half of the money was split equally among all 50 states. The remaining $25 billion was to be distributed based on certain metrics. Idaho’s low population density in rural communities and low density of rural healthcare providers were “challenges” for the scoring criteria, Charron said “Centers for Medicare and Medicaid had very specific criteria to drill down into: What does rural healthcare delivery look like in that specific state? And this is where we were a bit challenged, frankly, because we are so frontier in our state,” she said. Idaho scored highly for its existing state policies that align with Trump administration priorities, Charron said, including commitments to encourage the presidential fitness test in rural schools and changing the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, to ban purchases of candy and soda with it. items.body: Ashley and Joshua Durham used the Affordable Care Act marketplace for their health insurance after they began their family medicine practice in Boise, Idaho, in late 2023. But the couple say they opted out of health insurance for their family of four this year after they saw their ACA premium payments jump to nearly $1,600 a month. (Photo by Hayat Norimine/KFF Health News) This story was first published by KFF Health News on Sept. 22, 2026. Joshua and Ashley Durham run a family medicine practice, and for the first time in their lives, they have no health insurance. When the Durhams began their practice at the end of 2023 — he as a primary care physician and she as a pharmacist who handles the billing — the couple bought coverage for themselves and their two kids on the Affordable Care Act marketplace. But they said their monthly premiums for a similar health plan for this year rose several hundred dollars to nearly $1,600. Top insurance official recommends task force for studying Idaho’s most critical healthcare issues They decided to pay out-of-pocket for their medical expenses instead, leaning on $50,000 they had set aside in a health savings account over several years. “It’s nerve-racking,” said Joshua Durham, 47. “It just takes, you know, one little accident, and then you got a big fat bill.” The healthcare industry traditionally has more of its workforce on medical insurance than many other fields. Nationwide, 7% of all healthcare workers were uninsured in 2024, compared with 11% of all adults under 65, according to a KFF analysis of the most recent American Community Survey data. And doctors were especially unlikely to forgo health insurance, with just 2% uninsured. But even healthcare workers are feeling the pinch as health insurance costs rise each year, with employers expecting that costs will jump an additional 8.2% for 2027. The Republican-led Congress also opted last year not to renew Affordable Care Act marketplace credits enacted during the covid pandemic. While subsidies remain in place for people with low incomes, the pandemic-era credits helped reduce many consumers’ premium payments , especially those working in small businesses such as independent medical practices. Nearly half of marketplace enrollees worked for small businesses or were self-employed in 2024; some of the most common occupations included chiropractic care and dentistry. Jack Dillon, executive director of the Association for Independent Medicine , which represents 4,000 physician-led practices, said premium increases have become untenable for small businesses, whether employers seek coverage through the marketplace or directly from insurers. “The cost has become so astronomical,” Dillon said. “You’re looking at it and saying, ‘What’s the value?’” As health insurance continues to become less affordable, Dillon said, more healthcare employers may seek alternatives to their standard coverage, such as providing higher hourly wages or providing only minimal plans. The number of people without insurance in the U.S. is expected to increase by roughly 15 million over 10 years because of the expiration of the expanded ACA subsidies and $1.1 trillion in estimated cuts resulting from President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to the Congressional Budget Office. items.body: School funding was central to both candidates’ pitches at Tuesday’s state superintendent debate at the College of Idaho. Republican incumbent Debbie Critchfield touted her efforts this spring and summer to rewrite the state’s more than 30-year-old funding formula, her top priority if re-elected. She pointed to her relationships with legislators as key to passing a fund for high-needs students last legislative session, along with other education priorities. Those relationships, she said, will help her push a funding formula rewrite across the finish line next session if reelected. Democratic challenger Becky Sundin Mitchell emphasized enrollment-based funding and questioned whether Critchfield could succeed where previous state superintendents failed: getting lawmakers to approve a new K-12 funding formula. Sundin Mitchell stressed that Idaho’s public schools need more funds, in general, as they routinely rank 51st in the nation for per-pupil spending . She repeatedly called for legislators to spend more time in public schools. The debate, hosted by Idaho Education News and The College of Idaho, provided a glimpse into the candidates’ different approaches to school funding and a range of other issues, including the state superintendent’s role, a lingering special education funding gap, Idaho’s new private school tax credit law, and how much politics should shape education policy. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) A panel of federal appeals judges will soon decide whether to continue to allow full enforcement of Idaho’s abortion bans, or to allow a lower court’s previous ruling that provided more exemptions to the law. U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit Judges Kim McLane Wardlaw, Marsha Berzon and Consuelo Callahan heard oral arguments in a virtual hearing Tuesday afternoon. The state of Idaho, represented by an attorney from the conservative Christian legal advocacy group Alliance Defending Freedom , argued that the laws should be fully enforced as written. Idaho’s laws prohibit most abortions, except in cases to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors face felony penalties and civil lawsuits of a minimum of $20,000 if they perform the procedure outside those exemptions. ADF attorney Mathew Hoffmann argued that a lower court’s previous ruling that would’ve expanded exemptions to apply to serious health and mental health risks to the mother, was not grounded in historical precedent. He said there is no right to “therapeutic” abortions. Attorneys representing Boise maternal-fetal medicine specialist Dr. Stacy Seyb argued that an earlier court decision from U.S. District of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill should go back into effect. The ruling would’ve prevented the Ada County prosecutor and Idaho attorney general from enforcing Idaho’s abortion ban in cases where the mother’s health faced serious risk or her life was at risk due to self harm. Winmill later narrowed this block on enforcement to only protect abortions performed by Seyb. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador. (Photo courtesy of Attorney General Raúl Labrador) After Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed, a Ninth Circuit panel placed a hold on Winmill’s order, and the law went back into effect. Hoffmann said Winmill’s decision expanding the exemptions created “an abortion-on-demand regime.” “They leave it up to the subjective judgment of doctors to determine a risk sufficient to justify abortion,” he said. Stephanie Toti, executive director of the Lawyering Project, argued on behalf of Seyb that the expanded exemptions to the law were necessary. “The injunction entered by the district court in this case is narrow. It would enable only a small number of patients each year to obtain an abortion,” Toti said. “But for those patients, access to that care is vitally important, as the district court found.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. Hoffmann argued that it would not, because the Constitution does not explicitly provide a right to abortions. Toti argued that the 2022 decision did not mention rights to life and health, which she said are violated by the Idaho ban’s limited exemptions. Callahan questioned Toti over whether the request to allow abortions for serious risk of self harm was “weaker” than the other arguments. “We have a right to life, but you don’t have a right to kill yourself, right?” Callahan asked. items.body: The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State's Office, the University of Idaho's College of Law and Boise State University's Institute for Advancing American Values. (Photo by Getty Images) A new gathering aims to bring together policymakers, students and the public to discuss the U.S. Constitution’s protections for free speech and encourage civil discourse. The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State’s Office, the University of Idaho’s College of Law and Boise State University’s Institute for Advancing American Values , according to a Secretary of State’s Office press release. The keynote speaker for the event will be Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, who has championed Disagree Better, a national, nonpartisan initiative “designed to reduce inflammatory rhetoric and foster a culture of healthy debate,” according to its website. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. (Photo courtesy of Phil McGrane) “Free speech is fundamental to our system of government, but protecting it requires more than simply agreeing that it is important,” said Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. “It means listening to people we disagree with, defending their right to speak, and being willing to have difficult conversations. That is what we hope to accomplish with the Idaho Free Speech Summit.” Sessions at the summit will explore First Amendment issues “ranging from campaign finance and campus free speech to the broader challenges of maintaining civil discourse in an increasingly divided political environment,” the press release said. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson (left) listens as Gov. Spencer Cox holds a press conference to present his budget proposal at the Salt Lake County Library in Kearns, Utah, on Dec. 3, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Cox will talk about how Americans can disagree without abandoning strongly held beliefs, a theme he explores in his new book, “Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt,” according to the release. “We are pleased to be part of a discussion centered on one of our nation’s most important constitutional freedoms,” said Brian Kane, University of Idaho College of Law dean, in the release. “The University of Idaho College of Law is a natural partner for this conversation. Law schools should be places where difficult constitutional questions are examined carefully and where people learn how to engage seriously with ideas they may not share.” The daylong summit will have presentations and panel discussions, followed by an evening reception. A continuing legal education credit will also be available for participating attorneys. “Universities have an important role to play in creating spaces where people can wrestle with difficult questions and hear perspectives different from their own,” said Boise State University’s Andrew Finstuen in the release. “The Summit provides an opportunity to model the kind of thoughtful, constructive dialogue that is essential to a healthy civic culture.” Registration and additional information, including the Summit schedule and speaker lineup, are available at FreeSpeechIdaho.com . “Our goal isn’t to bring together people who all agree,” McGrane said in the release. “It is to bring together people who recognize that our constitutional freedoms are strongest when we defend the right of others to speak, listen to one another, and engage in good faith.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: A $7.9 million lab expansion is slated to begin this fall at Idaho State University’s Meridian campus — a project geared to support two partners seeking to address Idaho’s physician shortage. The project will add a 16-station human anatomy lab and a two-station embalming suite at the L.S. and Aline W. Skaggs Treasure Valley Anatomy and Physiology Laboratories. The building is home to a 34-station anatomy lab, Idaho State said in a news release. But demand is increasing, and the 6,130-square-foot remodel is designed to keep up with future growth. “We have a decade of very successful operations under our belt,” said Padma Gadepally, director of anatomy laboratories and clinical assistant professor at Idaho State. “We started with about 50 learners and now have upwards of 2,000 learners.” Existing lab space at the L.S. and Aline W. And in 2025, the adjacent Idaho College of Osteopathic Medicine increased enrollment by 75 students per cohort, increasing the need for the remodel. ICOM is the state’s sole medical school. “This project reflects our shared commitment to educating the next generation of healthcare professionals and ensuring Idaho communities have access to highly trained providers for years to come,” ICOM chair of anatomy Blaine Maley said in the Idaho State release. The expansion will also support another piece of Idaho’s medical education puzzle: a partnership between the University of Idaho and the University of Utah. The two universities are working on a medical education program at the U of I’s Boise campus, and their students would be able to use Idaho State’s new facilities. “This is the kind of partnership Idaho needs to grow its own healthcare workforce,” Rayme Geidl, co-director of the U of I School of Health and Medical Professions, said in the Idaho State release. “Collaborations like this show what’s possible when Idaho institutions work together.”
